newsitem.title: CHINA: China launches tax probe of foreign offices.
newsitem.headline: China launches tax probe of foreign offices.

text.p: China has launched a tax probe of foreign representative offices to halt suspected tax evasion, the Business Weekly reported on Sunday.
The probe started earlier this month and was expected to be completed by June next year, the newspaper quoted Su Xiaolu of the State Administration of Taxation as saying.

"The increase in tax revenue from the representative offices is much lower than the expansion of offices opened by foreign companies," said Su, head of the administration's foreign tax inspection division.
He said there were 7,000 registered representative offices in China -- compared with 1,000 in 1985 -- but the growth in tax revenue did not match the rise over this period.
The newspaper, published by the official China Daily, did not give any figures for tax revenues from representative offices.
China does not allow foreign representative offices to conduct operations that will produce revenue, limiting their role to that of a business coordinator.
But it taxes representative offices anyway, setting a rate based on their total expenses, and this has long been a source of friction.

Some representative offices had not registered with tax authorities while others used intermediaries to conduct business, the newspaper said. It said that a 1994 survey showed that more than 2,000 representative offices in Beijing alone had not registered with tax authorities.
Su said that tax authorities would select key offices for audit and serious offenders would be listed publicly. They would draft notices to specify what kinds of foreign representatives must pay tax.
They would also try to boost tax monitoring by stepping up coordination with other government departments, the newspaper said.
It added that hotels would be a focus of the effort. Companies that failed to register would not be allowed to rent hotel rooms for office space.
